To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The prevalence of HPV in HNSCC of the Waldeyers tonsillar ring is significantly higher than that of other HNSCC; (2) The prevalence of lymph node metastasis is higher in HPV-positive than in HPV-negative tumours, and (3) HPV-positive HNSCC patients have a better prognosis than HPV-negative patients with the same initial nodular status.
the prognosis of patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma is influenced by the presence of human papillomavirus in the tumour, but only in combination with other factors.
the prognosis of survival of HNSCC is influenced by the lymph node status, the anatomical location of the tumour, and the HPV infection of the tumour.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of HPV in HNSCC.
the role of the human papillomavirus (HPV) in the pathogenesis of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the head and the neck, and with the influence of HPV on prognosis and survival of patients with SCC.
the influence of HPV-infection on the clinical outcome of HNSCC.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HPV is not a decisive factor in the development of head and neck cancer.
the presence or absence of HPV infection is not the most important factor in determining the survival of patients with HNSC.

HPV infection in HNCC has no impact on survival of patients with HNCC, but that it can be used as a prognostic indicator for a better survival of patients with HPV-positive tumours, if they present with lymph node metastasis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of a high-risk HPV type in HNSCC of the Waldeyers ring is associated with a more favorable prognosis.
HPV infection is not an independent prognostic factor in HNSCC, but it is a prognostic factor for the response of the patients to therapy.
the HPV infection has no direct effect on the patient's overall survival, but that it has an influence on the survival of patients with lymph node metastasis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HPV-positive HNSCC patients have a better response to radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

HPV positivity is not a predictor of overall survival, but it is a predictor of survival in lymph node-positive patients, and that HPV-positive patients have better survival rates than HPV-negative patients with a similar lymph node status.
HPV-positive HNSCC patients with nodal metastasis have a better survival than HPV-negative HNSCC patients.
